items.readable_text:
Content:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio [MATH: r] takes the form
[MATH: a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_{n}]

Content:
The above formula states that to get to the next term in the sequence, we multiply the previous term by [MATH: r.]

Content:
To illustrate, consider the geometric sequence below:

Content:
[MATH: 1, \: 3, \: 9, \: 27, \: \dots]

Content:
The first term is [MATH: a_1=1,] and we can calculate the common ratio [MATH: r] as

Content:
[MATH: r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac 3 1 = 3.]

Content:
Therefore, the recursive formula is

Content:
[MATH: a_{n+1} = 3 \cdot a_{n} , \qquad a_1 = 1, \qquad n\geq 1.]

Content:
When writing out our final answer for the recursive formula, we should also state the first term and the range for [MATH: n.]

Content:
To check that the recursive formula is correct, we can use it to generate the next few terms of the series:

Content:
[MATH: a_{2}|= 3 ⋅ a_{1} = 3 ⋅ 1 = 30✓; a_{3}|= 3 ⋅ a_{2} = 3 ⋅ 3 = 90✓; a_{4}|= 3 ⋅ a_{3} = 3 ⋅ 9 = 27✓]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The recursive formula for a geometric sequence with common ratio [MATH: r] takes the form [MATH: a_{n+1} = r \cdot a_{n}.]

In this case, the first term is [MATH: a_1={\color{blue}1},] and we can calculate the common ratio [MATH: r] as

[MATH: r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac 4 1 = {\color{red}4}.]

Therefore, the recursive formula is

[MATH: a_{n+1} = {\color{red}4} \cdot a_{n} , \qquad a_1 = {\color{blue}1}, \qquad n\geq 1.]

items.title: Identifying Geometric Sequences

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

  1. [MATH: 10, \: 20, \: 30, \: 40, \: \dots]

  2. [MATH: a_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{6}a_n,\quad a_1 = 36,\quad n\geq 1]

  3. [MATH: f(n+1) = 2f(n)-1,\quad f(1) =2,\quad n\geq 1]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

1. [MATH: 10, \: 20, \: 30, \: 40, \: \dots]
2. [MATH: a_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{6}a_n,\quad a_1 = 36,\quad n\geq 1]
3. [MATH: f(n+1) = 2f(n)-1,\quad f(1) =2,\quad n\geq 1]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

  • Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term: [MATH: (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = (20)/(10)|= 2; (a_{3})/(a_{2}) = (30)/(20)|= (3)/(2)]

  • Sequence II is a geometric sequence. The recursive rule [MATH: a_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{6}a_n] tells us that each term is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{6}] times the previous term, so the common ratio is [MATH: r=\dfrac{1}{6}.]

  • Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first [MATH: 3] terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms. [MATH: f(1)|= 2; f(2)|= 2 ⋅ f(1) − 1 = 2 ⋅ 2 − 1 = 3; f(3)|= 2 ⋅ f(2) − 1 = 2 ⋅ 3 − 1 = 5] The first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios: [MATH: (f(2))/(f(1)) = (3)/(2); (f(3))/(f(2)) = (5)/(3)]

In conclusion, only sequence II is a geometric sequence.

Item 14 — Example: Identifying Geometric Sequences

Example Prompt:
Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

1. [MATH: 10, \: 20, \: 30, \: 40, \: \dots]
2. [MATH: a_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{6}a_n,\quad a_1 = 36,\quad n\geq 1]
3. [MATH: f(n+1) = 2f(n)-1,\quad f(1) =2,\quad n\geq 1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:
[MATH: (a_{2})/(a_{1}) = (20)/(10)|= 2; (a_{3})/(a_{2}) = (30)/(20)|= (3)/(2)]
- Sequence II is a geometric sequence. The recursive rule [MATH: a_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{6}a_n] tells us that each term is [MATH: \dfrac{1}{6}] times the previous term, so the common ratio is [MATH: r=\dfrac{1}{6}.]
- Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first [MATH: 3] terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms.
[MATH: f(1)|= 2; f(2)|= 2 ⋅ f(1) − 1 = 2 ⋅ 2 − 1 = 3; f(3)|= 2 ⋅ f(2) − 1 = 2 ⋅ 3 − 1 = 5]
The first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios:
[MATH: (f(2))/(f(1)) = (3)/(2); (f(3))/(f(2)) = (5)/(3)]

In conclusion, only sequence II is a geometric sequence.
